2022_246_troy_recommendation.paragraph: The Troy School District Facilities Review Committee delivered its final findings and bond recommendation to the Board of Education on May 3, 2022. Work products presented include a Facilities Condition Assessment putting total building needs at $220-250 Million, a district building inventory averaging 48 years old, and conceptual program estimates for all school facilities of $750,526,697 that the committee later refined to a $616,433,825 bond program total. The FRC recommended a $525 million bond program funded by a 2 mill increase to the current millage rate, placed on the November 8, 2022 ballot.
2022_246_troy_recommendation.page:
**What it is**
Slide deck titled "Presentation to the Board of Education," presented by the Troy School District Facilities Review Committee (FRC) on May 3, 2022, closing out the committee's Discovery / Exploration / Recommendation process and asking the Board to act on a bond proposal.

**Charge and membership**
The FRC is described as a decision-making body of TSD staff and community members charged with developing a plan for upgrading TSD educational facilities to support flexible, student-centered learning communities, and with producing a recommendation for the Board's consideration. Roughly 62 members are named, including Gayle Moran, Christian Muellar, Dawn Mulcahy, Brian Nutting, Matthew Olovson, Joe Pettinato, David Recker, Matt Sackrison, Sunil Sivaraman, Cornelius Godfrey, Ahmed Hakim, Stephen Hatfield, Hussein Irani, Ron Keoleian, Ramanathan Krishnamoorthy, Mark Moebus, Vital Anne, Kerry Brennan, Renee Burzynski, Mike Cottone, Bob Dowd, Roberto Garcia, Michael Giglio, Aparna Sriram, Swarnalatha Talluri, Lijo Thommana, John Tu, Kelsey Weatherspoon, Fiona Wingblad, Hong Ye, Brian Zawislak and Stephanie Zendler. Pre-committee "Stretch Your Thinking" work included student and teacher feedback, Cabinet and Board feedback, and a deep dive with administrative leaders led by Dr. Wagner.

**District facts**
Average building age 48 years old; roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings ("over 50 acres"); approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; approximately 500 acres of property, "roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area." Largest buildings listed are Athens (398,426 sq ft, 50 acres, opened 1974), THS (354,210 sq ft, 72 acres, opened 1992) and Baker (128,098 sq ft, 40 acres, opened 2006). Troy Union, opened 1925, is the oldest.

**Enrollment**
| Year | Enrollment | Year | Enrollment |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2011-12 | 12,312 | 2017-18 | 13,080 |
| 2012-13 | 12,438 | 2018-19 | 13,084 |
| 2013-14 | 12,573 | 2019-20 | 13,043 |
| 2014-15 | 12,553 | 2020-21 | 12,730 |
| 2015-16 | 12,556 | 2021-22 | 12,535 |
| 2016-17 | 12,889 | | |

**Facilities Condition Assessment**
Scope covered roofing, architectural systems, mechanical systems, electrical systems, site work (paving), site work (playgrounds/athletics) and security.

| Priority | Cost |
|---|---|
| Critical Needs (1-3 years) | $45-55 Million |
| Near Future Needs (4-6 years) | $90-100 Million |
| Future Needs (7-10 years) | $85-95 Million |
| TOTAL | $220-250 Million |

**Bond financing scenarios (30-year, three series)**
| Scenario | Total principal | Total interest | Avg millage | Total mills all debt | Increase in debt levy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Table_1c | $295,000,000 | $207,340,000 | 2.19 | 4.10 | 0.00 |
| Table_2c | $420,000,000 | $293,740,000 | 3.13 | 5.10 | 1.00 |
| Table_3c | $525,000,000 | $364,787,000 | 3.93 | 6.10 | 2.00 |
| Table_4c | $625,000,000 | $434,293,000 | 4.68 | 7.00 | 2.90 |

**Concepts, costing and survey**
Conceptual estimates began at $249,491,086 for elementary schools and $501,035,611 for secondary schools, $750,526,697 for all school facilities. Refinement produced $138,184,058 elementary and $436,249,767 secondary, plus $12,000,000 for buses and $30,000,000 for technology, for a $616,433,825 bond program total. A financial tolerance exercise found the greatest percentage at the $525 million mark, with 62% supporting $525M or higher and 38% supporting $420M or lower. An EPIC-MRA survey on the 2-mill proposal returned 66% Total YES and 27% Total NO. The committee formed consensus on an updated 2 mill Build including a $14,790,000 allocation to Troy High School upgrades.

**Recommendation**
A $525 million bond program, a 2 mill increase to the current millage rate, on the November 8, 2022 ballot. Taxpayer impact by Troy ZIP code: 48083 $300K average home market value / $300 annual / $25 monthly; 48084 $353K / $353 / $29; 48085 $392K / $392 / $33; 48098 $470K / $470 / $39.
2022_246_troy_recommendation.verbose:
Final report of the Troy School District Facilities Review Committee (FRC), presented to the Board of Education on May 3, 2022, recommending a $525 million bond program with a 2 mill increase to the current millage rate for the November 8, 2022 ballot.

**Committee charge.** The deck states that the Troy School District's Facilities Review Committee is a decision-making body inclusive of TSD staff and community members representing the diversity of the Troy community, charged with developing a plan for upgrading TSD educational facilities to support flexible, student-centered learning communities that meet the mission and vision of the District, and charged with developing a recommendation at the conclusion of its analysis for the Board of Education's consideration.

**Members.** Gayle Moran, Christian Muellar, Dawn Mulcahy, Brian Nutting, Matthew Olovson, Joe Pettinato, Michelle Phillips, Sarah Phillips, Namita Prasad, David Recker, Tonia Romancheck, Matt Sackrison, Sande Frisen, Sunil Sivaraman, Brian Smiatacz, Beth Soggs, Cornelius Godfrey, Julie Gould, Ahmed Hakim, Elizabeth Hammond, Stephen Hatfield, Alison Hendry, Kimberly Hoyle, Hussein Irani, Kelly Jones, Brian Kelly, Ron Keoleian, Erin Keyser, Ramanathan Krishnamoorthy, Briana Matti, Mark Moebus, Vital Anne, Michelle Barsh, Lauren Bestul, Kerry Brennan, Adam Burns, Renee Burzynski, Chris Centi, Mike Cottone, Scott Courtney, Jonathan Cross, Shaun Dantas, Bob Dowd, Mary Frederick, Tim Fulcher, Roberto Garcia, Michael Giglio, Aparna Sriram, Alyssa Stevens, Ann Sumnar, Swarnalatha Talluri, Debbie Taylor, Lijo Thommana, John Tu, Kelsey Weatherspoon, Alecia West, Nicole Wilson, Fiona Wingblad, Marie Woodman, Hong Ye, Brian Zawislak, Stephanie Zendler.

**Process.** Seven FRC meeting dates and tours are cited. Pre-FRC "Stretch Your Thinking" activities were student and teacher feedback on educational spaces, Cabinet and Board of Education feedback on their vision of education and current state of buildings, and a deep dive with administrative leaders conducted with Dr. Wagner. The path to the recommendation ran Discovery (understand district facilities, program, vision and modern learning), Exploration (examine whether buildings hinder or help the program vision and goals; evaluate and determine the best option), and Recommendation (recommend an option to the Board regarding a future bond program initiative). Discovery inputs listed were TSD Vision & Goals, Program Assessment, Facilities Condition Assessment, Today's Learning Environments, Community Sentiments, Curriculum Vision and District Overview.

**Building inventory.** Elementary buildings: Barnard, 18 acres, 64,192 sq ft, opened 1978, addition 2007; Bemis, 15.2 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1978, 2007; Costello, 23 acres, 52,055 sq ft, 1972, 2007; Hamilton, 15 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1983, 2007; Hill, 12.9 acres, 54,336 sq ft, 1967, additions 71-93-2006; Leonard, 16.1 acres, 59,220 sq ft, 1959, additions 68-94-2006; Martell, 14.2 acres, 52,799 sq ft, 1972, additions 92-2007; Morse, 9.8 acres, 54,636 sq ft, 1956, additions 62-68-94-2006; Schroeder, 10 acres, 61,896 sq ft, 1970, additions 93-2006; Troy Union, 21.8 acres, 66,929 sq ft, 1925, additions 53-70-90-2006; Wass, 21.4 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1978, 2007; Wattles, 19 acres, 59,150 sq ft, 1967, additions 78-2007. Middle schools: Baker, 40 acres, 128,098 sq ft, 2006; Boulan Park, 16 acres, 116,351 sq ft, 1971, 2015; Larson, 32 acres, 116,351 sq ft, 1971, 2015; Smith, 20.1 acres, 100,734 sq ft, 1967, additions 73-82-89-2007. High schools and other: Athens, 50 acres, 398,426 sq ft, 1974, additions 93-99-2006; Troy Learning Center (ITLC), 3 acres, 39,600 sq ft, 2020; THS, 72 acres, 354,210 sq ft, 1992, additions 2005-2015; IA East/TCT shared site with Baker, 91,455 sq ft, 1952, additions 55-67-70-78-80-19; Troy Preschool, 13.6 acres, 68,654 sq ft, 2019; Board Office, 15.5 acres, 12,000 sq ft, 1973, addition 1988; Services Building, shared site with Board, 29,143 sq ft, 2000; Transportation, 3.9 acres, 11,328 sq ft, 1964, 2007; Rankin, 1.5 acres, 24,696 sq ft.

**Fun facts.** Average building age 48 years old; roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, described as over 50 acres; approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; approximately 500 acres of property, roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**Enrollment trend.** 2011-12: 12,312; 2012-13: 12,438; 2013-14: 12,573; 2014-15: 12,553; 2015-16: 12,556; 2016-17: 12,889; 2017-18: 13,080; 2018-19: 13,084; 2019-20: 13,043; 2020-21: 12,730; 2021-22: 12,535. A debt millage rates chart is included as a graphic without extracted values.

**Facilities Condition Assessment.** Categories assessed were roofing, architectural systems, mechanical systems, electrical systems, site work (paving), site work (playgrounds/athletics) and security. Cost summary by priority: Critical Needs (1-3 years) $45-55 Million; Near Future Needs (4-6 years) $90-100 Million; Future Needs (7-10 years) $85-95 Million; TOTAL $220-250 Million. A program assessment graded all buildings against attributes of modern learning environments on a Good / Needs Improvement / Poor scale.

**Bond financing.** Estimated bonding capacity was modeled as a 30-year bond in three series at a 4.00% estimated interest rate. Table_1c: Series 2023 $70,000,000 over 29 yrs., 3 mo. with $48,843,000 estimated total interest cost and $9,450,000 amortized within the first 6 years; Series 2026 $90,000,000 over 30 yrs., 0 mo. with $63,284,000 interest and $9,925,000; Series 2029 $135,000,000 over 30 yrs., 0 mo. with $95,213,000 interest and $13,925,000; total $295,000,000 principal, $207,340,000 interest, first-year millage 1.23, average millage 2.19, total mills all debt 4.10, increase in debt levy 0.00. Table_2c: $110,000,000 / $75,901,000 / $19,925,000; $135,000,000 / $96,061,000 / $14,025,000; $175,000,000 / $121,778,000 / $19,500,000; total $420,000,000 principal, $293,740,000 interest, 2.20 first-year millage, 3.13 average millage, 5.10 total mills, 1.00 increase. Table_3c: $150,000,000 / $100,583,000 / $30,075,000; $175,000,000 / $121,905,000 / $20,175,000; $200,000,000 / $142,299,000 / $20,550,000; total $525,000,000 principal, $364,787,000 interest, 3.19 first-year millage, 3.93 average millage, 6.10 total mills, 2.00 increase. Table_4c: $185,000,000 / $124,042,000 / $38,700,000; $210,000,000 / $146,276,000 / $26,750,000; $230,000,000 / $163,975,000 / $24,375,000; total $625,000,000 principal, $434,293,000 interest, 4.08 first-year millage, 4.68 average millage, 7.00 total mills, 2.90 increase.

**Guiding principles, ranked.** 1 Flexible & Adaptable Learning Spaces; 2 Spaces that Encourage Curiosity & Exploration; 3 Flexible Furniture; 4 Technology; 5 Student Collaboration Space; 6 Smaller Learning Communities; 7 Abundant Natural Light; 8 Interdisciplinary Collaboration; 9 Acoustics - Quiet Spaces/Sensory; 10 Accessibility/Universal Design; 11 Upgrade Performing Arts / Athletic Spaces; 12 Career / Partnerships; 13 Strong Visual Image / Brand Identity; 14 Professional Collaboration Space; 15 Eco-Friendly; 16 Playground Upgrades; 17 Access that is direct, safe & welcoming; 18 Gross Motor Development.

**Conceptual estimates and refinement.** Original conceptual estimates: elementary schools $249,491,086; secondary schools $501,035,611; all school facilities $750,526,697. Revised conceptual estimates: elementary schools $138,184,058; secondary schools $436,249,767; buses, not included in the original estimate, $12,000,000; technology, previously rolled into school estimates, $30,000,000; bond program total $616,433,825 against the original $750,526,697.

**Financial tolerance and survey.** The financial tolerance exercise found the greatest percentage falling at the $525 million mark, with 62% supporting $525M or higher and 38% supporting $420M or lower. A professional survey conducted by EPIC-MRA asked respondents how they would vote on the 2-mill proposal, pressing undecided respondents on whether they would lean YES or NO if the election were held today: 66% Total YES and 27% Total NO, with reported bar values of 52% and 14% on the Yes side, 21% and 6% on the No side, and 7% undecided. Voter progression across proposals showed solid YES of 52%, 58% and 60% and lean YES of 14%, 21% and 24% for the 2-Mill, 1-Mill and 0-Mill proposals, with 66% Total YES, 79% Total YES and 84% Total YES respectively. Feedback analysis noted very consistent thinking across the 2 mill Build and individual selections, one major area of difference being THS academic remodeling, and consensus on allocating renovation dollars to THS without going to the $49M level. The FRC then formed consensus around a new 2 mill Build that included an allocation of $14,790,000 to upgrades at Troy High School.

**Recommendation.** The committee cited over 700 hours of time invested by committee members, 7 Steering Committee meetings, tours of district schools, the EPIC-MRA professional survey, and development and analysis of various ideas, concepts and estimates. Its recommendation: a $525 million bond program; a 2 mill increase to the current millage rate; a proposal on the November 8, 2022 ballot, stated as transforming school facilities to support the future of education and allow Troy School District to continue to provide a World Class Education for ALL.

**Building-level scope.** Every elementary school (Barnard, Bemis, Hamilton, Wass, Costello, Martell, Hill, Leonard, Morse, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wattles) receives infrastructure upgrades per the foundational elements matrix plus accessibility/universal design upgrades to all toilet rooms, new flexible adaptable furniture, playground replacement with new surfaces and accessible equipment, and space (new or remodel) for a 3rd Kindergarten classroom. Morse adds a new art room/general storage addition; Troy Union adds 4 new classrooms to replace removed original structure. Baker Middle School remodels its media center as multi-use space for interdisciplinary collaboration/STEM/robotics. Boulan Park and Larson Middle Schools reconfigure all classrooms and the media center for interdisciplinary collaboration/STEM/robotics with proper sizing, glass walls, and staff and student collaboration spaces. Smith Middle School gets a new 2-story school of 120,000 square feet for 750 students including space for STEM/robotics. Athens High School gets a new 3-level academic wing and major remodeling of remaining academic areas. Troy High School gets upgrades addressing circulation issues, student collaboration enhancements, multi-use space for robotics, fitness and other activities, other identified critical program needs, and expanded plus new music rehearsal spaces. International Academy East and Troy Center for Transition receive toilet room accessibility work and new furniture; Troy Career & College High School receives toilet room accessibility work. District support buildings receive roof replacement, window and exterior door replacement, new ceilings and flooring where needed, toilet partitions and accessories, casework replacement, LED lighting upgrades, replacement of aging mechanical units and plumbing fixtures, exhaust fan replacement, temperature controls, upgraded electrical service and power panels, access control/intrusion detection, asphalt paving replacement and partial concrete walkway replacement.

**Taxpayer impact.** For the $525 million program at a 2 mill increase, by Troy ZIP code: 48083 average home market value $300K, $300 annual and $25 monthly impact; 48084 $353K, $353 and $29; 48085 $392K, $392 and $33; 48098 $470K, $470 and $39.

2022_247_8_d_pq_june_2022_troy_sd_5_10_2.paragraph: Preliminary Qualification financial workbook (Form 3881) for the Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, with financial information as of 5/10/2022, prepared by Paul Stauder of PFM Financial Advisors LLC. It supports a proposed $555,000,000 unlimited-tax general obligation bond issue over a 30-year term at a 4.00% average interest rate, carrying $398,981,000 of interest, to be issued in three series of $167,000,000, $188,000,000 and $200,000,000 for a November 8, 2022 election. Against $116,165,000 of existing bond debt levied at 4.10 mills, the filing projects a total estimated millage of 6.10 for the next tax year and a first-year millage increase of 2.00.

2022_248_frc_presentation_051722.paragraph: Second delivery of the Troy School District Facilities Review Committee's report to the Board of Education, dated May 17, 2022, restating the committee's charge, its Facilities Condition Assessment total of $220-250 Million, and conceptual estimates that moved from $750,526,697 to a refined $616,433,825 bond program total. The recommendation stands at a $525 million bond program with a 2 mill increase to the current millage rate on the November 8, 2022 ballot, including a $14,790,000 allocation to Troy High School upgrades.
2022_248_frc_presentation_051722.page:
**What it is**
"Presentation to the Board of Education" by the Troy School District Facilities Review Committee, dated May 17, 2022 - the FRC deck brought back to the Board two weeks after its May 3 delivery, with sustainability added to the Facilities Condition Assessment scope and an additional district initiatives slide.

**Committee and process**
The FRC is described as a decision-making body of TSD staff and community members charged with developing a plan for upgrading TSD educational facilities to support flexible, student-centered learning communities and producing a recommendation for the Board. Roughly 62 members are named, among them Gayle Moran, Dawn Mulcahy, Joe Pettinato, Namita Prasad, Matt Sackrison, Cornelius Godfrey, Elizabeth Hammond, Hussein Irani, Ron Keoleian, Ramanathan Krishnamoorthy, Vital Anne, Kerry Brennan, Mike Cottone, Bob Dowd, Roberto Garcia, Aparna Sriram, Swarnalatha Talluri, Lijo Thommana, John Tu, Fiona Wingblad, Hong Ye and Stephanie Zendler. Seven meeting dates and school tours are cited, along with pre-FRC feedback from students, teachers, Cabinet and Board and a deep dive with administrative leaders conducted with Dr. Wagner. The path ran Discovery, Exploration and Recommendation.

**District facts**
Average building age 48 years old; roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, over 50 acres; approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; approximately 500 acres of property, roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area. Athens is the largest building at 398,426 sq ft on 50 acres (opened 1974); THS 354,210 sq ft on 72 acres (1992); Troy Union, opened 1925, is the oldest.

**Enrollment**
2011-12 through 2021-22: 12,312; 12,438; 12,573; 12,553; 12,556; 12,889; 13,080; 13,084; 13,043; 12,730; 12,535.

**Facilities Condition Assessment**
Categories: roofing, architectural systems, mechanical systems, electrical systems, site work (paving), site work (playgrounds/athletics), security and sustainability.

| Priority | Cost |
|---|---|
| Critical Needs (1-3 years) | $45-55 Million |
| Near Future Needs (4-6 years) | $90-100 Million |
| Future Needs (7-10 years) | $85-95 Million |
| TOTAL | $220-250 Million |

**Bond financing scenarios**
| Scenario | Total principal | Total interest | Avg millage | Total mills | Levy increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Table_1c | $295,000,000 | $207,340,000 | 2.19 | 4.10 | 0.00 |
| Table_2c | $420,000,000 | $293,740,000 | 3.13 | 5.10 | 1.00 |
| Table_3c | $525,000,000 | $364,787,000 | 3.93 | 6.10 | 2.00 |
| Table_4c | $625,000,000 | $434,293,000 | 4.68 | 7.00 | 2.90 |

**Estimates and survey**
Original conceptual estimates: elementary $249,491,086, secondary $501,035,611, all school facilities $750,526,697. Revised: elementary $138,184,058, secondary $436,249,767, buses $12,000,000, technology $30,000,000, bond program total $616,433,825. Financial tolerance results place the greatest percentage at the $525 million mark, 62% supporting $525M or higher and 38% supporting $420M or lower. EPIC-MRA survey results on the 2-mill proposal: 66% Total YES, 27% Total NO. Voter progression shows 66% Total YES on the 2-Mill proposal, 79% on the 1-Mill and 84% on the 0-Mill.

**Recommendation and taxpayer impact**
Over 700 hours of committee time, 7 Steering Committee meetings, school tours and an EPIC-MRA professional survey led to the recommendation of a $525 million bond program, a 2 mill increase, on the November 8, 2022 ballot. Taxpayer impact: 48083 $300K home value / $300 annual / $25 monthly; 48084 $353K / $353 / $29; 48085 $392K / $392 / $33; 48098 $470K / $470 / $39.
2022_248_frc_presentation_051722.verbose:
Facilities Review Committee report delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on May 17, 2022, a second presentation of the committee's Discovery-Exploration-Recommendation work following the May 3, 2022 delivery. Content is substantially the same deck, with sustainability listed among the Facilities Condition Assessment categories, a Bond Program Estimate slide, and a slide adding district initiatives beyond building work.

**Charge.** The Troy School District's Facilities Review Committee is described as a decision-making body inclusive of TSD staff and community members representing the diversity of the Troy community, charged with developing a plan for upgrading TSD educational facilities to support flexible, student-centered learning communities that meet the mission and vision of the District, and with developing a recommendation at the conclusion of its analysis for the Board of Education's consideration.

**Members.** Gayle Moran, Christian Muellar, Dawn Mulcahy, Brian Nutting, Matthew Olovson, Joe Pettinato, Michelle Phillips, Sarah Phillips, Namita Prasad, David Recker, Tonia Romancheck, Matt Sackrison, Sande Frisen, Sunil Sivaraman, Brian Smiatacz, Beth Soggs, Cornelius Godfrey, Julie Gould, Ahmed Hakim, Elizabeth Hammond, Stephen Hatfield, Alison Hendry, Kimberly Hoyle, Hussein Irani, Kelly Jones, Brian Kelly, Ron Keoleian, Erin Keyser, Ramanathan Krishnamoorthy, Briana Matti, Mark Moebus, Vital Anne, Michelle Barsh, Lauren Bestul, Kerry Brennan, Adam Burns, Renee Burzynski, Chris Centi, Mike Cottone, Scott Courtney, Jonathan Cross, Shaun Dantas, Bob Dowd, Mary Frederick, Tim Fulcher, Roberto Garcia, Michael Giglio, Aparna Sriram, Alyssa Stevens, Ann Sumnar, Swarnalatha Talluri, Debbie Taylor, Lijo Thommana, John Tu, Kelsey Weatherspoon, Alecia West, Nicole Wilson, Fiona Wingblad, Marie Woodman, Hong Ye, Brian Zawislak, Stephanie Zendler.

**Process.** Seven FRC meeting dates and tours are noted. Pre-FRC "Stretch Your Thinking" activities were student and teacher feedback to gain perspective on educational spaces, Cabinet and Board of Education feedback on their vision of education and the current state of buildings, and a deep dive with administrative leaders with Dr. Wagner. Discovery covered TSD vision and goals, program assessment, facilities condition assessment, today's learning environments, community sentiments, curriculum vision and district overview. Exploration examined whether buildings hinder or help the program vision and goals and evaluated the best option to meet the vision. Recommendation delivered an option to the Board regarding a future bond program initiative.

**Building inventory.** Barnard, 18 acres, 64,192 sq ft, opened 1978, addition 2007; Bemis, 15.2 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1978, 2007; Costello, 23 acres, 52,055 sq ft, 1972, 2007; Hamilton, 15 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1983, 2007; Hill, 12.9 acres, 54,336 sq ft, 1967, additions 71-93-2006; Leonard, 16.1 acres, 59,220 sq ft, 1959, additions 68-94-2006; Martell, 14.2 acres, 52,799 sq ft, 1972, additions 92-2007; Morse, 9.8 acres, 54,636 sq ft, 1956, additions 62-68-94-2006; Schroeder, 10 acres, 61,896 sq ft, 1970, additions 93-2006; Troy Union, 21.8 acres, 66,929 sq ft, 1925, additions 53-70-90-2006; Wass, 21.4 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1978, 2007; Wattles, 19 acres, 59,150 sq ft, 1967, additions 78-2007; Baker, 40 acres, 128,098 sq ft, 2006; Boulan Park, 16 acres, 116,351 sq ft, 1971, 2015; Larson, 32 acres, 116,351 sq ft, 1971, 2015; Smith, 20.1 acres, 100,734 sq ft, 1967, additions 73-82-89-2007; Athens, 50 acres, 398,426 sq ft, 1974, additions 93-99-2006; Troy Learning Center (ITLC), 3 acres, 39,600 sq ft, 2020; THS, 72 acres, 354,210 sq ft, 1992, additions 2005-2015; IA East/TCT on a shared site with Baker, 91,455 sq ft, 1952, additions 55-67-70-78-80-19; Troy Preschool, 13.6 acres, 68,654 sq ft, 2019; Board Office, 15.5 acres, 12,000 sq ft, 1973, addition 1988; Services Building on a shared site with the Board Office, 29,143 sq ft, 2000; Transportation, 3.9 acres, 11,328 sq ft, 1964, 2007; Rankin, 1.5 acres, 24,696 sq ft.

**Fun facts.** Average building age 48 years old; roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, described as over 50 acres; approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; approximately 500 acres of property, roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**Enrollment trend.** 2011-12: 12,312; 2012-13: 12,438; 2013-14: 12,573; 2014-15: 12,553; 2015-16: 12,556; 2016-17: 12,889; 2017-18: 13,080; 2018-19: 13,084; 2019-20: 13,043; 2020-21: 12,730; 2021-22: 12,535. A debt millage rates slide is included as a graphic.

**Facilities Condition Assessment.** Categories assessed: roofing, architectural systems, mechanical systems, electrical systems, site work (paving), site work (playgrounds/athletics), security and sustainability. Cost summary by priority: Critical Needs (1-3 years) $45-55 Million; Near Future Needs (4-6 years) $90-100 Million; Future Needs (7-10 years) $85-95 Million; TOTAL $220-250 Million. The program assessment graded all buildings against attributes of modern learning environments as Good, Needs Improvement or Poor.

**Bond financing scenarios.** Estimated bonding capacity for a 30-year bond, all series priced at a 4.00% estimated interest rate. Table_1c: Series 2023 $70,000,000 over 29 yrs., 3 mo., $48,843,000 estimated total interest cost, $9,450,000 amortized within the first 6 years; Series 2026 $90,000,000 over 30 yrs., 0 mo., $63,284,000, $9,925,000; Series 2029 $135,000,000 over 30 yrs., 0 mo., $95,213,000, $13,925,000; total $295,000,000 and $207,340,000, first-year millage 1.23, average millage 2.19, total mills all debt 4.10, increase in debt levy 0.00. Table_2c: $110,000,000 / $75,901,000 / $19,925,000; $135,000,000 / $96,061,000 / $14,025,000; $175,000,000 / $121,778,000 / $19,500,000; total $420,000,000 and $293,740,000, 2.20 first-year millage, 3.13 average millage, 5.10 total mills, 1.00 increase. Table_3c: $150,000,000 / $100,583,000 / $30,075,000; $175,000,000 / $121,905,000 / $20,175,000; $200,000,000 / $142,299,000 / $20,550,000; total $525,000,000 and $364,787,000, 3.19 first-year millage, 3.93 average millage, 6.10 total mills, 2.00 increase. Table_4c: $185,000,000 / $124,042,000 / $38,700,000; $210,000,000 / $146,276,000 / $26,750,000; $230,000,000 / $163,975,000 / $24,375,000; total $625,000,000 and $434,293,000, 4.08 first-year millage, 4.68 average millage, 7.00 total mills, 2.90 increase.

**Guiding principles, ranked.** 1 Flexible & Adaptable Learning Spaces; 2 Spaces that Encourage Curiosity & Exploration; 3 Flexible Furniture; 4 Technology; 5 Student Collaboration Space; 6 Smaller Learning Communities; 7 Abundant Natural Light; 8 Interdisciplinary Collaboration; 9 Acoustics - Quiet Spaces/Sensory; 10 Accessibility/Universal Design; 11 Upgrade Performing Arts / Athletic Spaces; 12 Career / Partnerships; 13 Strong Visual Image / Brand Identity; 14 Professional Collaboration Space; 15 Eco-Friendly; 16 Playground Upgrades; 17 Access that is direct, safe & welcoming; 18 Gross Motor Development.

**Conceptual estimates and refinement.** Original conceptual estimates: elementary schools $249,491,086; secondary schools $501,035,611; all school facilities $750,526,697. Revised conceptual estimates: elementary schools $138,184,058; secondary schools $436,249,767; buses, not included in the original estimate, $12,000,000; technology, previously rolled into school estimates, $30,000,000; bond program total $616,433,825.

**Financial tolerance and survey.** The financial tolerance exercise found the greatest percentage falling at the $525 million mark, with 62% supporting $525M or higher and 38% supporting $420M or lower. The EPIC-MRA survey asked how respondents would vote on the 2-mill proposal, with undecided respondents pressed on whether they would lean YES in favor of the bond proposal or NO to oppose it if the election were held today; results were 66% Total YES and 27% Total NO, with chart values of 52% and 14% on the Yes side, 21% and 6% on the No side, and 7% undecided. Voter progression showed solid YES of 52%, 58% and 60% and lean YES of 14%, 21% and 24% for the 2-Mill, 1-Mill and 0-Mill proposals, totaling 66% Total YES, 79% Total YES and 84% Total YES. Analysis of feedback recorded very consistent thinking across the 2 mill Build and individual selections, one major area of difference being THS academic remodeling, and consensus on wanting to allocate renovation dollars to THS without going to the $49M level. The FRC then formed consensus around a new 2 mill Build that included an allocation of $14,790,000 to upgrades at Troy High School.

**Recommendation.** Citing over 700 hours of committee time, 7 Steering Committee meetings, tours of district schools, the professional survey conducted by EPIC-MRA, and development and analysis of various ideas, concepts and estimates, the FRC recommended a $525 million bond program, a 2 mill increase to the current millage rate, and a proposal on the November 8, 2022 ballot, stating the program will transform school facilities to support the future of education and allow Troy School District to continue to provide a World Class Education for ALL.

**Building-level scope.** All twelve elementary schools - Barnard, Bemis, Hamilton, Wass, Costello, Martell, Hill, Leonard, Morse, Schroeder, Troy Union and Wattles - receive infrastructure upgrades per the foundational elements matrix plus accessibility and universal design upgrades to all toilet rooms, new flexible adaptable furniture, playground replacement with new surfaces and accessible equipment, and space (new or remodel) for a 3rd Kindergarten classroom. Morse additionally receives a new art room and general storage addition; Troy Union receives 4 new classrooms to replace removed original structure. Baker Middle School remodels its media center into multi-use space for interdisciplinary collaboration, STEM and robotics. Boulan Park and Larson Middle Schools reconfigure all classrooms and the media center for interdisciplinary collaboration, STEM and robotics with proper sizing, glass walls and added staff and student collaboration spaces. Smith Middle School receives a new 2-story school of 120,000 square feet for 750 students including space for STEM and robotics. Athens High School receives a new 3-level academic wing and major remodeling of remaining academic areas. Troy High School receives upgrades addressing circulation issues, student collaboration enhancements, multi-use space for robotics, fitness and other activities, other identified critical program needs, and expanded plus new music rehearsal spaces. International Academy East and Troy Center for Transition receive toilet room accessibility work and new furniture; Troy College and Career High School receives toilet room accessibility work.

**District support buildings and additional initiatives.** Facilities Condition Assessment upgrades for support buildings cover roof replacement, window and exterior door replacement, new ceilings and flooring where needed, toilet partitions and accessories, casework replacement, LED lighting upgrades, replacement of aging mechanical units and plumbing fixtures, exhaust fan replacement, temperature controls, upgraded electrical service and power panels, interior LED lighting, access control and intrusion detection, asphalt paving replacement and partial concrete walkway replacement. Additional district initiatives listed are purchase of buses, special education programming upgrades and technology upgrades.

**Taxpayer impact.** For the $525 million program with a 2 mill increase, by Troy ZIP code: 48083, average home market value $300K, annual impact $300, monthly impact $25; 48084, $353K, $353, $29; 48085, $392K, $392, $33; 48098, $470K, $470, $39. The deck closes by thanking the Board for the opportunity to present the work of the FRC.
